title: Hoon Lee on Expanding His Character in East of Eden
excerpt:
The actor praises Zoe Kazan's interpretation of John Steinbeck's novel.
He argues that the expanded role reflects the book's central themes.
body_md:
Hoon Lee has expressed relief and gratitude over the reception of East of Eden, Zoe Kazan's adaptation of John Steinbeck's novel starring Florence Pugh. The series premiered in October 2026, carrying the considerable expectations associated with a celebrated literary work.

One of its major changes is the expansion of Lee's story. Kazan and writer Alexander Chee developed a standalone episode for the character, with the resulting footage ultimately incorporated into other episodes. Lee knew his role would be expanded but discovered its extent when he received the scripts.

The actor considers the additions consistent with Steinbeck's exploration of human agency, choice and dignity. He credits Kazan's detailed knowledge of the novel and believes her interpretation is grounded in the material rather than arbitrary invention.

Lee also argues that a literal one-to-one adaptation is impossible. Readers construct their own imagined worlds and priorities, whereas screen productions collectively determine what audiences see and where their attention is directed.

He contrasted the new series with Elia Kazan's 1950s film starring James Dean, which omitted Lee entirely. For the actor, the omission reflects a different interpretation of what mattered most in the novel, while the new production offers another perspective.

Lee regards playing the character as an honor and emphasizes the importance of truth and human complexity. His broader argument is that enduring stories benefit from periodic reinterpretation, even when audiences disagree about individual creative choices.
